newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe dogged by Chirac's contradictions.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe dogged by Chirac's contradictions.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whose centre-right government took office in May 1995 pledging to reduce crippling unemployment, is set to face voters at an early election with the jobless rate higher than ever.

That is only one of the many paradoxes facing Juppe, saddled with the task of reconciling President Jacques Chirac's contradictory campaign promises to simultaneously create jobs, lower taxes and cut public deficits.
Judging by his inaugural policy address, the relentless climb of unemployment to 12.8 from 11.7 percent when he was appointed would appear to condemn Juppe out of his own mouth.
"We want to be judged, when the time comes, on our ability to stimulate in France a deep and durable movement to create jobs," he told parliament days after taking power.

Juppe launched into an expensive, double-barrelled programme aimed to cut youth and long-term unemployment, create 700,000 jobs, lift the minimum wage, raise pensions and create new benefits for the elderly and children.

This populist effort was coupled with reforms meant to reassure international financial markets that included payroll charge reductions, a value added tax increase and accelerated privatisations of state owned companies.

But in October 1995, under pressure from financial markets and a worried Germany, Chirac was forced to shelve his promises of quick job creation and tax cuts, switching to austerity to qualify for a single European currency.
"The priority of priorities is to cut deficits," he said, conceding he had underestimated France's financial problems.

The turnaround, likened to the late president Francois Mitterrand's abandonment of doctrinaire socialism for fiscal orthodoxy in 1983, was followed by a cabinet reshuffle and the launch of a plan to reform the welfare state.

The plan was deeply unpopular and sent Chirac's and Juppe's popularity ratings plunging to historic lows. Juppe retained the president's full support despite becoming the most unpopular prime minister in France's history.

The curbs on welfare spending, coupled with an ill-prepared plan to streamline the state railways, triggered a strike by public sector workers that crippled the country for nearly a month in November and December 1995.

Juppe was forced to shelve the rail reform and abandon some key elements of his social security plan, notably a provision to make public employees work longer for a full pension, although he has stuck to his core goal of limiting the increase in public health spending.
It was the first of several bouts of labour unrest to plague his government.
Doctors, bank employees, medical students and civil servants have struck against any attempt to trim their "acquired rights" or hold them to account for overspending on public health.

Truck drivers blockaded the country's roads last November to win the right to retirement at 55 and improvements in their harsh working conditions. But a bid by some trade unions to widen the demand for earlier retirement to other sectors failed.
After raising the tax burden by an estimated 120 billion francs ($20.9 billion) in his first 15 months in office, Juppe announced a five-year plan to cut income tax rates last September.
But local authority taxes have continued to rise as the central government has shifted more of the burden of public spending to local government.
An ambitious privatisation programme begun by Juppe's predecessor Edouard Balladur stalled, with few major successes other than the sales of aluminum giant Pechiney and insurance company AGF.
Plans to restructure a large part of the defence sector have run into trouble over the sale of Thomson-CSF and the planned merger and privatisation of plane-maker Aerospatiale and Dassault Aviation.
Troubled state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais with its billions of francs of losses has been a thorn in the government's side epitomising the struggles of France's loss-ridden financial sector.
